title: Participating Presences
content_html:
Participating presences

Photographs and paintings are not biologically alive - they don’t metabolize, reproduce, or evolve. They’re physical artifacts: pigment, paper, pixels, or digital data. But they can be alive phenomenologically, relationally, and symbolically. In the phenomenological sense (relating to experience), an image feels alive when it evokes movement, presence, or emotion. A portrait may “look back” at you, landscapes can “breathe,” and abstract works can feel dynamic. Our brains are tuned to see life everywhere (pareidolia, animism). A still face in a photo can trigger recognition of aliveness because facial perception taps into specialized neural circuits. In a philosophical sense (relating to representation and memory), a photo or painting can extend the life of what it depicts - preserving memory and presence beyond biological time. In this way, it’s a vessel of lived experience. Some traditions hold that images participate in the life of their subjects: they’re not inert but carry essence, spirit, or agency.

In phenomenology and Buddhist thought, “aliveness” is not intrinsic but relational. An image is alive in relation to your consciousness. It becomes animated through your act of perception. John Berger (in Ways of Seeing) suggests paintings live differently in each viewer’s gaze, renewed each time they’re seen. Roland Barthes (in Camera Lucida) writes that a photograph is both “that-has-been” and “still-here,” a paradox of life and death. It’s alive because it insists on the existence of a moment that once lived. Many painters (for example, Van Gogh, Rothko, Pollock) sought to capture not just forms but vitality - “life itself” in paint.

Art holds memory, presence, and even agency in cultural or spiritual frameworks. Its “aliveness” is less about what they are than what they do - how they engage perception, stir memory, and transmit vitality.

Artworks are not just objects but “indexes”: they mediate social relations, acting as if they had agency. For example, a carved ancestor figure is not only a representation; it acts as a social agent - binding kin groups, mediating rituals, even causing fear or reverence. The term “distributed personhood” suggests that the life of a subject can extend into an image or object, as if part of their being is lodged there. This view resists the Western modernist division between inert matter (art) and active life (humans). Instead, images participate in networks of action and meaning.

Many indigenous traditions don’t draw a hard line between image, subject, and spirit. In Australian Aboriginal art, rock paintings and sand drawings aren’t just depictions but part of Dreaming (ancestral creation). They are alive, continually re-activated in ritual and storytelling. In Andean and Amazonian traditions woven patterns and painted ceramics are treated as carriers of spirit and cosmological knowledge. They “speak” or “remember” the forces of nature. In **African masking traditions, **a mask becomes the spirit or ancestor when danced. The image does not merely stand in - it is the subject in a new form. This worldview is sometimes described as animist: objects and images are alive with spirit, agency, or relational force.

In these frameworks, images are not inert symbols but participating presences. They can protect, heal, or curse; transmit ancestral power; make the absent present (ancestors, deities, spirits). To interact with such an image is to enter into relation with the being it embodies. The image is not “about” something; it is a locus where subject, spirit, and community converge. Even in the West, echoes of this appear:

Catholic icons and relics: paintings of saints or statues of the Virgin Mary are often treated as if they contain presence - hence miracles associated with them; photographs in mourning: as Roland Barthes suggested, a photo can feel like the presence of the loved one; people often speak to photos as if to the person. This suggests that the sense of an image carrying life is not foreign to modernity, though often disavowed by rationalist frameworks.

These traditions challenge the Western “representational” model of art (image as inert sign). They support a relational ontology: life, spirit, and agency are distributed across humans, objects, and images. This dovetails with Actor-Network Theory (Bruno Latour): agency is shared between humans and non-humans, and the Buddhist emptiness (śūnyatā): things have no independent essence but arise in relation. An image’s “life” exists only in co-arising with subject, viewer, and context.

In summary, for many traditions images are extensions of life itself. They don’t simply depict but actively participate in the being of what they represent. They are “alive” because they carry, transmit, or enact the presence, spirit, or agency of their subjects.
